title: World History: Medieval & Early Modern (7th Grade)
description: World History: Medieval & Early Modern (7th Grade) practice - 100 questions

questions.correctAnswer: 476 CE
questions.explanation: In 476 CE the Germanic leader Odoacer removed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Roman Empire, however, continued for almost another thousand years.

img.scene: Ancient Roman city scene with a toppled marble column and a cracked imperial statue in the foreground, legion banners lowered, dramatic dusk light, historical illustration.
img.tip: The Western Empire fell in 476 CE; the East endured.
img.title: THE FALL OF ROME - 476 CE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 476 - the West took its final bow.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire fall, an event historians often use to mark the start of the medieval period?

questions.correctAnswer: The Byzantine Empire
questions.explanation: The eastern half of the Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, preserved Roman law and Greek learning and lasted until 1453.

img.scene: Golden-domed Byzantine capital city on a strait with ships, great walls and a famous domed cathedral, sunrise, historical illustration.
img.tip: Constantinople kept Roman law and culture alive in the East.
img.title: THE BYZANTINE EMPIRE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rome fell in the West, but its eastern twin lived on.
questions.question: After Rome fell in the West, which empire carried on Roman government, law, and culture in the East?

questions.correctAnswer: It sat on trade routes linking Europe and Asia
distractors: It had the largest army in the world
It was built entirely of gold
It never had to pay taxes
questions.explanation: Constantinople controlled the strait between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, so merchants moving goods between Europe and Asia passed through its markets and paid its tolls.

img.scene: Busy medieval harbor market at a strait with merchant ships, cranes unloading silk bales and spice sacks, merchants in varied dress, historical illustration.
img.tip: Constantinople grew rich taxing Europe-Asia trade.
img.title: CROSSROADS OF TRADE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Constantinople was the toll booth between two continents.
questions.question: Why was Constantinople such a wealthy and powerful city?

questions.correctAnswer: Organize Roman laws into a single code
questions.explanation: Justinian's Code gathered and organized centuries of Roman law into one system. It became the foundation of legal systems in much of Europe.

img.scene: Byzantine scholars in a marble hall sorting tall stacks of law scrolls into neat shelves while an emperor observes, historical illustration.
img.tip: One organized law code became Europe's legal foundation.
img.title: JUSTINIAN'S CODE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Justinian put Rome's messy laws into one tidy code.
questions.question: Emperor Justinian is best remembered for ordering a team of scholars to do what?

questions.correctAnswer: Church architecture with a massive dome
distractors: A royal palace of pure gold
questions.explanation: Completed in 537 CE, the Hagia Sophia's enormous dome seemed to float above the church floor, an engineering marvel that inspired builders for centuries.

img.scene: Interior of a vast domed cathedral with light streaming through a ring of windows under the dome, tiny worshippers below, historical illustration.
img.tip: Its giant dome was an engineering marvel of 537 CE.
img.title: HAGIA SOPHIA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Hagia Sophia's dome looked like it floated on light.
questions.question: The Hagia Sophia in Constantinople was famous in the medieval world mainly as a remarkable example of what?

questions.correctAnswer: Invading peoples, political instability, and an overstretched army
distractors: A single plague that killed everyone
Running out of farmland in one year
questions.explanation: Historians point to combined pressures: Germanic peoples pressing the borders, emperors overthrown in rapid succession, and an army too small to defend a huge frontier.

img.scene: Roman frontier scene with legionaries guarding a long border wall while migrating peoples with wagons approach from beyond, historical illustration.
img.tip: Invasions, instability, and thin defenses combined to fell Rome.
img.title: PRESSURE ON AN EMPIRE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rome did not fall to one blow - it was squeezed from all sides.
questions.question: Which set of problems weakened the Western Roman Empire before it fell?

questions.correctAnswer: They spread Orthodox Christianity and created a written alphabet for Slavic languages
distractors: They taught them to build castles
questions.explanation: Missionaries such as Cyril and Methodius devised an alphabet for Slavic languages and translated religious texts, spreading both literacy and Orthodox Christianity.

img.scene: Two Byzantine monk-missionaries teaching Slavic villagers, one holding a parchment with a new alphabet, a wooden church behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: Byzantine missionaries gave Slavic peoples an alphabet.
img.title: FAITH AND LETTERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The missionaries brought the Slavs faith - and letters.
questions.question: How did Byzantine missionaries affect the Slavic peoples of Eastern Europe?

questions.correctAnswer: Ottoman forces captured Constantinople
distractors: A massive earthquake destroyed the city
Its own people voted to dissolve it
questions.explanation: Sultan Mehmed II's Ottoman army used huge cannons to breach Constantinople's famous walls in 1453, ending the empire after more than a thousand years.

img.scene: Medieval siege scene with enormous bronze cannons firing at massive city walls beside a harbor chain, banners flying, historical illustration.
img.tip: Ottoman cannons breached Constantinople's walls in 1453.
img.title: 1453 - THE CITY FALLS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In 1453, giant cannons ended a thousand-year empire.
questions.question: What finally ended the Byzantine Empire in 1453?

questions.correctAnswer: Greek
questions.explanation: Although the empire began as Roman, Greek gradually replaced Latin in government, church, and scholarship in the East.

img.scene: Byzantine classroom scene with a teacher and students reading Greek scrolls, mosaic walls behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: Greek replaced Latin in Byzantine government and learning.
img.title: GREEK IN THE EAST

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The eastern empire spoke Greek, not Latin.
questions.question: Which language remained the main language of government and learning in the Byzantine Empire?

questions.correctAnswer: The Great Schism
questions.explanation: Disputes over authority and practice led the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople to excommunicate each other in 1054, dividing Christianity into western Catholic and eastern Orthodox branches.

img.scene: Two church leaders in different vestments turning away from each other across a marble table with a torn parchment, historical illustration.
img.tip: Christianity split into Catholic West and Orthodox East.
img.title: THE GREAT SCHISM - 1054

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In 1054, one church split into West and East.
questions.question: The split between the Roman Catholic Church in the West and the Orthodox Church in the East, finalized in 1054, is known as what?

questions.correctAnswer: In Arabia, in southwest Asia
questions.explanation: Islam began in the Arabian Peninsula, in the cities of Mecca and Medina, and spread from there across southwest Asia and beyond.

img.scene: Seventh-century Arabian desert city with mud-brick houses, palm trees, camel caravans and a busy market square, historical illustration.
img.tip: The faith began in Mecca and Medina in the 600s CE.
img.title: ISLAM BEGINS IN ARABIA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Islam began in Arabia's desert cities.
questions.question: On which continent and in which region did Islam begin in the 600s CE?

questions.correctAnswer: The Prophet Muhammad
questions.explanation: Muslims believe the angel Gabriel revealed God's words to Muhammad, a merchant from Mecca, beginning around 610 CE. Followers later recorded these revelations as the Qur'an.

img.scene: A lone figure in simple robes seen from behind, standing at a cave entrance on a rocky mountain above a desert city at dawn, respectful historical illustration without showing the face.
img.tip: Muslims believe he received the Qur'an's revelations.
img.title: THE PROPHET MUHAMMAD

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Muhammad received the revelations of the Qur'an.
questions.question: Who do Muslims believe received the revelations that became the Qur'an?

questions.correctAnswer: Giving charity to the poor (zakat)
distractors: Building a mosque in every city
questions.explanation: The Five Pillars are the declaration of faith, prayer five times daily, charity to the poor, fasting during Ramadan, and the hajj pilgrimage to Mecca for those who are able.

img.scene: Five tall stone pillars supporting a graceful arched roof, worshippers praying below, a charity box and a crescent above, symbolic historical illustration.
img.tip: Faith, prayer, charity, fasting, and pilgrimage.
img.title: THE FIVE PILLARS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One pillar is giving - charity holds up the faith.
questions.question: Which of the following is one of the Five Pillars of Islam?

questions.correctAnswer: It marks the start of the Muslim calendar and of the first Muslim community
distractors: It is the year the Qur'an was printed
It is the year Islam reached Spain
It is the year Muhammad was born
questions.explanation: The journey, called the Hijra, began the first community governed by Islamic teaching in Medina, so Muslims count their calendar years from 622 CE.

img.scene: Travelers on camels crossing desert dunes at dawn toward a distant palm oasis city, historical illustration.
img.tip: The move to Medina began the first Muslim community.
img.title: THE HIJRA - 622 CE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Hijra to Medina starts the Muslim calendar.
questions.question: Why is the year 622 CE, when Muhammad moved from Mecca to Medina, so important in Islam?

questions.correctAnswer: Most of the Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal)
questions.explanation: By the early 700s, Muslim armies and rulers controlled North Africa and most of Iberia, where Islamic culture flourished in cities such as Cordoba for centuries.

img.scene: Medieval Iberian city with a grand arched mosque, orange groves and scholars carrying books, mountains behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: By the early 700s, Muslim rule reached Spain.
img.title: EXPANSION TO IBERIA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Within a century, Islam reached all the way to Spain.
questions.question: Within about a hundred years of Muhammad's death, Muslim rule had expanded to include which far-western region?

questions.correctAnswer: They preserved Greek texts and advanced mathematics, medicine, and astronomy
distractors: They banned the study of science
questions.explanation: Scholars in cities like Baghdad translated and preserved Greek and Roman works and made their own advances - including algebra and improved astronomical tables - which later flowed into Europe through Spain and Sicily.

img.scene: Great medieval library hall with translators copying scrolls, an astronomer with an astrolabe, and stacks of manuscripts, historical illustration.
img.tip: Baghdad scholars preserved Greek works and advanced science.
img.title: HOUSE OF WISDOM

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Baghdad's scholars saved old books and wrote new science.
questions.question: How did Muslim scholars of this era contribute to learning in Europe?

questions.correctAnswer: Arabic-language scholarship building on Indian numerals
distractors: Chinese merchants on the Silk Road only
questions.explanation: Indian mathematicians developed the numerals; Arabic-speaking scholars adopted and spread them along with algebra, and Latin translations carried both into Europe.

img.scene: Medieval scholar writing equations and numerals on parchment while merchants with goods from distant lands wait at the door, historical illustration.
img.tip: Indian numerals spread through Arabic scholarship to Europe.
img.title: NUMBERS ON THE MOVE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Our numbers traveled India to Arabia to Europe.
questions.question: The word 'algebra' and the numerals used in most of the world today reached Europe largely through which route?

questions.correctAnswer: The pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims should make once in their lifetime if able
questions.explanation: The hajj gathers millions of pilgrims in Mecca each year. Its shared rituals connect Muslims from every country to one community of faith.

img.scene: Vast crowd of pilgrims in white garments circling a large cube-shaped shrine draped in black cloth in a grand courtyard, historical illustration.
img.tip: The pilgrimage to Mecca unites Muslims worldwide.
img.title: THE HAJJ

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The hajj brings the world to Mecca.
questions.question: What is the hajj?

questions.correctAnswer: The split between Sunni and Shia Muslims
distractors: The split between Arabs and Persians
questions.explanation: Sunni Muslims accepted leaders chosen by the community; Shia Muslims held that leadership belonged to Muhammad's family, beginning with his cousin and son-in-law Ali. The division continues today.

img.scene: A road forking into two paths in a desert landscape, two groups of travelers taking different routes toward distant cities, symbolic historical illustration.
img.tip: A dispute over leadership divided the Muslim community.
img.title: SUNNI AND SHIA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: One question - who leads? - split Islam into Sunni and Shia.
questions.question: After Muhammad's death, disagreement over who should lead the Muslim community led to which lasting division?

questions.correctAnswer: A minaret, the tower from which the call to prayer is announced
distractors: A bell tower with a cross
questions.explanation: The minaret is the slender tower of a mosque. From it, the call to prayer rings out five times a day over the surrounding neighborhood.

img.scene: Elegant mosque with a tall slender minaret and dome at sunset in a medieval city, birds circling the tower, historical illustration.
img.tip: From the minaret, the call to prayer sounds five times daily.
img.title: THE MINARET

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The minaret calls the faithful to prayer.
questions.question: Which feature appears on nearly every mosque, helping worshippers know when to pray?

questions.correctAnswer: Gunpowder
questions.explanation: Chinese alchemists searching for an elixir of life instead found gunpowder. Song armies used it in bombs and early rockets, and the technology later spread westward.

img.scene: Medieval Chinese workshop with alchemists, powder barrels, and early fire-arrows being tested in a courtyard, historical illustration.
img.tip: Song China used gunpowder in bombs and rockets.
img.title: GUNPOWDER

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Gunpowder was an accident that changed every battlefield.
questions.question: Which Chinese invention of the Tang and Song eras most changed warfare in later centuries?

questions.correctAnswer: To select government officials based on merit and learning
distractors: To choose army generals by strength
To test merchants for trading licenses
questions.explanation: Candidates spent years studying Confucian classics, then competed in difficult written exams. Success opened government careers to talented men beyond the highest-born families.

img.scene: Rows of small individual exam booths in a vast courtyard filled with scholars writing at desks, officials watching, historical illustration.
img.tip: Difficult exams selected officials by merit and learning.
img.title: THE EXAM SYSTEM

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pass the exam, earn the office - merit over birth.
questions.question: What was the purpose of China's civil service examination system under the Tang and Song dynasties?

questions.correctAnswer: Movable-type printing
questions.explanation: Song printers carved characters onto movable blocks that could be rearranged for each page, making books far cheaper than copying by hand.

img.scene: Song dynasty print workshop with racks of small carved character blocks and workers pressing inked pages, historical illustration.
img.tip: Rearrangeable blocks made books cheaper and more common.
img.title: MOVABLE TYPE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Movable type put books in many more hands.
questions.question: Which Chinese invention helped spread books and learning during the Song dynasty?

questions.correctAnswer: Merchants found heavy strings of coins impractical for large trade
distractors: China ran out of metal entirely
The emperor wanted his portrait everywhere
Paper was sacred in Chinese religion
questions.explanation: Copper coins were so heavy that merchants in Sichuan began using paper receipts; the Song government took over issuing official paper notes, the world's first government paper money.

img.scene: Medieval Chinese market scene with a merchant exchanging a paper note at a money-changer's stall, strings of round coins stacked nearby, historical illustration.
img.tip: Song China issued the first government paper currency.
img.title: THE FIRST PAPER MONEY

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Coins got too heavy, so China printed money.
questions.question: Why did paper money first appear in Song China?

questions.correctAnswer: Linking the rice-growing south with the political north for trade and taxes
questions.explanation: The canal connected the Yangtze and Yellow river regions, letting southern rice and goods flow to northern capitals cheaply by boat instead of overland.

img.scene: Long canal with grain barges passing through a lock gate between green rice paddies and a distant city, historical illustration.
img.tip: The canal linked the rice-rich south to northern capitals.
img.title: THE GRAND CANAL

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Grand Canal fed the north with southern rice.
questions.question: The Grand Canal, expanded under the Sui and Tang, mainly helped China by doing what?

questions.correctAnswer: The magnetic compass
questions.explanation: Chinese sailors used the magnetic compass to hold a course far from land, expanding sea trade across Asia and later to the wider world.

img.scene: Medieval Chinese junk ship at sea with a sailor checking a small floating-needle compass bowl, sails full, historical illustration.
img.tip: The compass let sailors navigate far from land.
img.title: THE COMPASS AT SEA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The compass pointed sailors across open oceans.
questions.question: Which Chinese invention most helped sailors navigate accurately on long ocean voyages?

questions.correctAnswer: Silk, porcelain, and technology flowed west while gold, glass, and ideas flowed east
distractors: Only silk ever moved in either direction
Armies used it, but no merchants did
It carried goods only between Chinese cities
questions.explanation: The routes were an exchange network, not a one-way street: Chinese goods and inventions traveled west, while Central Asian and European goods, religions, and ideas traveled into China.

img.scene: Desert Silk Road caravan with camels carrying silk bales passing a watchtower, oasis ahead, historical illustration.
img.tip: Goods and ideas moved in both directions.
img.title: THE SILK ROAD

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Silk Road traded in both directions - goods and ideas.
questions.question: Which statement best describes trade along the Silk Road during the Tang and Song periods?

questions.correctAnswer: Porcelain
questions.explanation: Chinese porcelain was so fine, white, and durable that it became a prized luxury worldwide - in English, fine dishes are still called 'china.'

img.scene: Chinese porcelain workshop with painters decorating white vases with blue designs, kilns behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: Fine dishes are still called 'china' today.
img.title: PORCELAIN

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The world's finest dishes were literally called china.
questions.question: Which Chinese product was so prized in foreign markets that its name became the everyday word for fine dishes?

questions.correctAnswer: A capital where foreign merchants, monks, and fashions mixed with Chinese culture
distractors: A city closed to all foreigners
questions.explanation: Tang Chang'an, perhaps the world's largest city then, hosted merchants and monks from Persia, India, and Central Asia, making it a crossroads of goods and ideas.

img.scene: Grand Tang dynasty capital avenue with markets, foreign merchants in varied dress, Buddhist monks and a pagoda, historical illustration.
img.tip: Chang'an was a world crossroads of goods and ideas.
img.title: CHANG'AN, WORLD CITY

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Chang'an was the world's meeting place.
questions.question: The Tang capital, Chang'an, is best described as which of the following?

questions.correctAnswer: It blended Confucian ethics with Buddhist and Daoist ideas and became the official philosophy of later China
distractors: It was only a style of painting
It lasted for a single year
questions.explanation: Thinkers such as Zhu Xi reinterpreted Confucius in light of centuries of Buddhist and Daoist thought, producing a philosophy that shaped Chinese education and government for 700 years.

img.scene: Song scholar teaching students under a pavilion, scrolls open, a garden blending ordered paths and natural rocks, historical illustration.
img.tip: Neo-Confucianism shaped Chinese thought for 700 years.
img.title: NEO-CONFUCIANISM

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Neo-Confucianism remixed Confucius for a new age.
questions.question: Neo-Confucianism, which developed during the Song dynasty, is best described how?

questions.correctAnswer: Taxing the gold and salt traded across its land
questions.explanation: Ghana sat between northern salt mines and southern gold fields. Its kings grew rich by taxing caravans moving both goods through their territory.

img.scene: West African market scene with camel caravans, slabs of salt and gold dust being weighed on scales, a king's officials collecting tolls, historical illustration.
img.tip: Ghana taxed both sides of the gold-salt trade.
img.title: GHANA'S GOLD AND SALT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ghana got rich standing between gold and salt.
questions.question: The kingdom of Ghana in West Africa grew wealthy mainly by doing what?

questions.correctAnswer: People in hot regions needed it to survive, and it preserved food
distractors: It was used to make weapons
It was rarer than gold underground
questions.explanation: In the hot Sahel, people lose salt through sweat and needed it to stay healthy; before refrigeration, salt also kept meat and fish from spoiling. In some markets it traded ounce for ounce with gold.

img.scene: Saharan salt mine with workers cutting large white salt slabs while camels wait to carry them south, historical illustration.
img.tip: Salt preserved food and kept people healthy in the heat.
img.title: WHY SALT WAS TREASURE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No salt, no health - and no preserved food.
questions.question: Why was salt nearly as valuable as gold in medieval West Africa?

questions.correctAnswer: Mansa Musa
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa ruled Mali at its height in the 1300s. His famous pilgrimage to Mecca displayed Mali's gold wealth to North Africa and the Middle East.

img.scene: A West African emperor in golden robes riding with a huge retinue of camels loaded with goods through a desert town, historical illustration.
img.tip: His pilgrimage showed Mali's wealth to the world.
img.title: MANSA MUSA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mansa Musa's golden journey made Mali famous.
questions.question: Which ruler made the empire of Mali famous across Africa and the Islamic world with his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324?

questions.correctAnswer: He spent and gave away so much gold that its price fell there for years
distractors: He built a canal to the Nile
questions.explanation: Passing through Cairo, Mansa Musa's generous gifts and spending flooded the market with gold, and chroniclers report its value stayed depressed for about a decade.

img.scene: Busy Cairo street scene with crowds around a caravan distributing gold gifts, merchants examining coins, historical illustration.
img.tip: His generosity flooded Cairo with gold.
img.title: GOLD IN CAIRO

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mansa Musa gave away so much gold, prices dropped for years.
questions.question: What happened in Cairo during Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage?

questions.correctAnswer: A center of Islamic learning, trade, and book copying
questions.explanation: At the edge of the Sahara, Timbuktu linked desert caravans to river trade and grew famous for its mosques, universities, and libraries of hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.

img.scene: Timbuktu scene with mud-brick mosque towers, scholars carrying manuscripts, and camel caravans arriving at dusk, historical illustration.
img.tip: Timbuktu was a city of scholars and manuscripts.
img.title: TIMBUKTU

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Timbuktu traded in books as much as gold.
questions.question: The city of Timbuktu in Mali became famous across the medieval world as what?

questions.correctAnswer: Family libraries preserved hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on astronomy, law, medicine, and mathematics
distractors: Books were forbidden in the city
All books were written in Latin
questions.explanation: Libraries in Timbuktu - many kept by families for centuries - show that medieval West Africa had a deep written culture in science and law, not only oral tradition.

img.scene: Interior of a Timbuktu library with wooden shelves of leather-bound manuscripts, a scholar reading by lamplight, historical illustration.
img.tip: Its libraries held hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.
img.title: LIBRARIES OF TIMBUKTU

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Timbuktu's families guarded whole libraries of science.
questions.question: Which fact about Timbuktu challenges the idea that medieval Africa had no written scholarship?

questions.correctAnswer: Camels
questions.explanation: Camels can travel days without water and carry heavy loads over sand, making regular caravans across the Sahara possible.

img.scene: Long camel caravan crossing golden Sahara dunes at sunrise, drivers walking beside loaded animals, historical illustration.
img.tip: Camels made regular Sahara crossings possible.
img.title: SHIPS OF THE DESERT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Camels were the trucks of the Sahara.
questions.question: Trans-Saharan trade depended on which animal, uniquely suited to long desert journeys?

questions.correctAnswer: Controlling the crossroads and taxing goods passing through brought steady wealth without owning the mines
distractors: They owned every gold mine in Africa
They refused all contact with traders
questions.explanation: Ghana and Mali did not need to own the gold fields. By securing routes and markets and taxing each caravan, their kings turned geography into revenue.

img.scene: A caravan toll station at a desert crossroads with officials, scales and stacked goods, royal banners flying, historical illustration.
img.tip: Taxing trade at the crossroads was steady revenue.
img.title: POWER AT THE CROSSROADS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Own the crossroads, tax the trade, skip the digging.
questions.question: How did Ghana's and Mali's rulers profit from trade routes they did not fully control at both ends?

questions.correctAnswer: They memorized and retold histories, genealogies, and traditions aloud
distractors: They carved laws into stone pillars
They printed the first African newspapers
questions.explanation: In societies where much history was kept orally, griots were trained from childhood to remember centuries of royal genealogies and events - living archives whose accounts historians still use, cross-checked with written sources.

img.scene: A griot storyteller playing a stringed instrument before a fire-lit village gathering, listeners of all ages around, historical illustration.
img.tip: Griots were living archives of West African history.
img.title: THE GRIOTS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Griots carried whole libraries in memory.
questions.question: What was the role of griots in West African societies such as Mali?

questions.correctAnswer: A mountainous island nation off East Asia's coast
questions.explanation: Japan is an archipelago of mountainous islands. The sea separated it from the mainland, while mountains divided its people into local communities.

img.scene: Aerial view of green mountainous islands surrounded by sea, small coastal villages and rice terraces, historical illustration.
img.tip: Mountains and sea shaped Japan's local societies.
img.title: ISLANDS OF JAPAN

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Japan's mountains and seas shaped its feudal map.
questions.question: Which description best fits Japan's geography, which shaped its medieval society?

questions.correctAnswer: Shinto
questions.explanation: Shinto centers on kami, spirits of nature and ancestors, honored at shrines. It remained Japan's native faith even after Buddhism arrived from the mainland.

img.scene: A red shrine gate in a forest with a small shrine building, visitors bowing respectfully, cherry blossoms falling, historical illustration.
img.tip: Shinto honors kami, spirits of nature and ancestors.
img.title: SHINTO

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Shinto honors the spirits in nature and ancestors.
questions.question: Japan's native religion, focused on reverence for nature spirits called kami, is called what?

questions.correctAnswer: The emperor was the symbolic head, while the shogun held real military and political power
distractors: The shogun was a religious priest only
The emperor personally led every battle
There was no emperor during this period
questions.explanation: From 1192, shoguns ruled Japan in the emperor's name. The emperor kept sacred status at court in Kyoto while the shogunate governed from its own headquarters.

img.scene: Split scene: a serene imperial court with a seated emperor on one side and a military headquarters with banners and commanders on the other, historical illustration.
img.tip: The emperor symbolized; the shogun governed.
img.title: EMPEROR AND SHOGUN

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The emperor reigned, but the shogun ruled.
questions.question: In feudal Japan, what was the relationship between the emperor and the shogun?

questions.correctAnswer: Bushido, the warrior's code of honor, loyalty, and discipline
distractors: Chivalry only, with no other name
questions.explanation: Bushido - 'the way of the warrior' - demanded loyalty to one's lord, courage, and self-discipline, much as chivalry guided European knights.

img.scene: A samurai in armor kneeling before his lord in a castle hall, katana placed respectfully before him, historical illustration.
img.tip: Bushido demanded loyalty, courage, and discipline.
img.title: BUSHIDO

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Bushido was the samurai's code of honor.
questions.question: The samurai class in Japan followed which code of conduct?

questions.correctAnswer: Powerful local lords who controlled land and their own samurai
questions.explanation: Daimyo ruled their domains almost independently, building castles and armies of samurai, and owed loyalty to the shogun - a structure much like Europe's feudal lords.

img.scene: A fortified Japanese castle town with a daimyo's banner, samurai patrols and rice fields below, historical illustration.
img.tip: Daimyo were Japan's powerful regional lords.
img.title: THE DAIMYO

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Daimyo were Japan's great local lords.
questions.question: Who were the daimyo in feudal Japan?

questions.correctAnswer: Writing characters, Buddhism, and styles of government and architecture
questions.explanation: Japanese missions to Tang China brought back adapted Chinese characters, Buddhist schools, and models for capitals and administration - which Japan then reshaped to fit its own traditions.

img.scene: Japanese envoys on a ship arriving at a Chinese port city, carrying scrolls and gifts, pagodas in both styles behind, historical illustration.
img.tip: Japan borrowed writing, Buddhism, and government models.
img.title: LEARNING FROM CHINA

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Japan borrowed from China, then made it its own.
questions.question: Which set of ideas did Japan borrow most heavily from China during this era?

questions.correctAnswer: It adopted foreign ideas selectively and adapted them to Japanese traditions
distractors: It copied China in every detail
questions.explanation: Japan's borrowing was deliberate: missions chose what to import, and over time the Japanese stopped the official missions and developed distinct arts, writing (kana), and institutions.

img.scene: A Japanese scribe writing flowing kana script beside Chinese characters on a scroll, cherry branch in a vase nearby, historical illustration.
img.tip: Japan adapted imports like kana writing to its own ways.
img.title: SELECTIVE BORROWING

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Japan borrowed carefully - and customized everything.
questions.question: Which statement best describes Japan's borrowing from China and Korea?

questions.explanation: Parish churches marked every village's calendar, marriages, and holidays; church courts set moral rules; and for centuries the clergy were among the few who could read and write.

questions.correctAnswer: Associations of craftspeople that set standards, prices, and training
questions.explanation: A guild controlled its craft in a town: it trained apprentices, inspected quality, and protected members' livelihoods - a cornerstone of the growing medieval towns.

questions.explanation: Gothic engineering shifted weight outward through flying buttresses, so walls could open into soaring stained-glass windows that filled cathedrals with colored light.

questions.correctAnswer: Workers became scarce, so surviving peasants could demand higher wages and more freedom
distractors: Lords gained total power over peasants
questions.explanation: The plague killed roughly a third of Europe's people. With labor suddenly precious, peasants bargained for wages and freedom, and serfdom faded across much of western Europe.

distractors: They printed books for all of Europe

questions.explanation: Monks copied books by hand in scriptoriums, keeping classical and religious texts alive through centuries when few others could read - and monasteries also sheltered travelers and the sick.

questions.explanation: As trade revived, lords and kings could hire soldiers and officials with money instead of granting land for service. Plague-driven labor bargaining and growing royal courts finished much of the old system.

img.title: WHY LUTHER SUCCEEDED

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Press plus princes - that is why Luther lasted.
questions.question: Earlier critics of the Church, like Jan Hus, were executed. Why did Luther's movement survive?

questions.correctAnswer: To find faster sea routes to Asia's spices and goods after land routes grew costly
distractors: To find the fountain of youth
questions.explanation: Spices and silks reached Europe through many middlemen, raising prices sharply. Portugal and Spain funded voyages to reach India and China directly by sea.

img.scene: A 1400s harbor with caravels being loaded, sacks of spices and charts on the dock, sailors preparing rigging, historical illustration.
img.tip: Sea routes promised cheaper spices and silk.
img.title: WHY SAIL WEST?

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Europe sailed to cut out the spice middlemen.
questions.question: Why did European nations fund risky ocean voyages in the late 1400s?

questions.correctAnswer: Columbus reached the Americas in 1492 while seeking a westward route to Asia
distractors: Columbus proved the Earth was flat
questions.explanation: Sailing for Spain, Columbus crossed the Atlantic and landed in the Caribbean, believing he had reached Asia. His voyages opened sustained contact between Europe and the Americas - with devastating consequences for Native peoples.

img.scene: Three small sailing ships anchored off a tropical island coast, landing boats approaching the beach, historical illustration.
img.tip: 1492 opened lasting Europe-America contact.

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Columbus aimed for Asia and found a new world of contact.
questions.question: What happened in 1492 during Columbus's first voyage?

questions.correctAnswer: The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, and people between the Americas and the rest of the world
distractors: A trade fair held in Spain
The exchange of gold for silver only
A treaty between Portugal and Spain
questions.explanation: Corn, potatoes, and tomatoes transformed diets in Europe, Africa, and Asia; horses and cattle changed the Americas; and European diseases devastated Native populations who had no immunity.

img.scene: A harbor scene with two ships exchanging goods - corn, potatoes and tomatoes one way, horses and wheat the other, historical illustration.
img.tip: Foods, animals, and diseases crossed both ways.
img.title: THE COLUMBIAN EXCHANGE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Exchange moved whole worlds of food - and disease.
questions.question: What was the Columbian Exchange?

questions.correctAnswer: The first voyage around the entire Earth
distractors: The first crossing of the Atlantic
questions.explanation: Magellan's expedition (1519-1522) crossed the Pacific and returned to Spain under Elcano after Magellan's death, proving the scale of the Earth and the connection of its oceans.

img.scene: A battered sailing ship with patched sails entering a home harbor after a long voyage, crowds on the quay, historical illustration.
img.tip: One ship completed the first trip around the world.
img.title: AROUND THE WORLD

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Magellan's crew finished the first lap around Earth.
questions.question: Magellan's expedition of 1519-1522 is famous for completing what?

questions.correctAnswer: Small Spanish forces, aided by Native allies and diseases, toppled the Aztec and Inca empires
distractors: The empires had already vanished centuries earlier
The Aztecs invited Spain to rule them
questions.explanation: Cortes (1519-1521) and Pizarro (1530s) exploited political divisions, allied with subject peoples, and benefited from steel weapons, horses, and smallpox epidemics that shattered both empires.

img.scene: A small column of Spanish soldiers and many Native allies marching toward a great lake city, mountains beyond, historical illustration.
img.tip: Alliances and disease decided the conquests.
img.title: THE CONQUESTS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Allies and epidemics, not numbers, toppled empires.
questions.question: How did Cortes and Pizarro conquer the vast Aztec and Inca empires with relatively few men?

questions.correctAnswer: Copernicus
questions.explanation: In On the Revolutions (1543), Copernicus placed the Sun at the center, reviving an ancient idea with new mathematics - a model later evidence from Galileo and Kepler strongly supported.

img.scene: An astronomer at a desk with a model of planets circling a central sun, star charts and a window open to the night sky, historical illustration.
img.tip: Copernicus put the Sun at the center in 1543.
img.title: THE SUN AT THE CENTER

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Copernicus moved the Earth - on paper first.
questions.question: Which astronomer proposed that the Earth revolves around the Sun, challenging the ancient Earth-centered model?

questions.correctAnswer: It gave direct evidence against the old model, and the Church forced him to recant under threat
questions.explanation: Galileo's telescope revealed Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus - hard evidence for the new astronomy. In 1633 the Inquisition tried him and he recanted publicly, though his work spread anyway.

img.scene: An astronomer looking through a long telescope at Jupiter from a rooftop at night, a small sketch of four moons on his desk, historical illustration.
img.tip: Jupiter's moons backed the new astronomy with evidence.
img.title: GALILEO'S TELESCOPE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Galileo's moons made the old model impossible.
questions.question: What happened when Galileo published his telescopic discoveries supporting Copernicus?

questions.correctAnswer: One law of universal gravitation explaining both falling objects and planetary orbits
questions.explanation: Newton's Principia (1687) showed the same gravity that pulls an apple also guides the Moon and planets, uniting earthly and heavenly motion under mathematical laws - the capstone of the Scientific Revolution.

img.scene: A scholar beneath an apple tree gazing up at the Moon, an orbit diagram drawn in an open notebook, historical illustration.
img.tip: One gravity law rules apples and planets alike.
img.title: NEWTON'S GRAVITY

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Newton: one law for the apple and the Moon.
questions.question: What was Isaac Newton's great unifying idea?

questions.correctAnswer: Thinkers applied reason and natural rights to argue governments need the people's consent
distractors: Kings' power was declared unlimited by reason
questions.explanation: Locke argued people have natural rights and may change unjust governments; Montesquieu proposed separating powers. These Enlightenment ideas fed directly into the American and French revolutions closing the period in 1789.

img.scene: Enlightenment thinkers debating in a bright salon with books, a model balance of scales and columns symbolizing separated powers, historical illustration.
img.tip: Reason and rights reshaped ideas of government.
img.title: THE ENLIGHTENMENT

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reason asked: why should kings rule without consent?
questions.question: By 1789, how were Enlightenment ideas changing political thought in Europe and America?
